content: Christmas Seals are adhesive labels that are affixed to envelopes during the Christmas season with the purpose of raising funds and increasing awareness for tuberculosis programs. In 1904, Einar Holbøll, a Danish postal clerk, conceived the idea of using seals on envelopes during Christmas to generate financial support for combating tuberculosis. This initiative received approval from the Postmaster and the King of Denmark. The first seal featured the likeness of the Queen and the word Julen, which means Christmas. Over four million seals were sold in the first year. In 1907, Emily Bissell introduced the concept of Christmas Seals to the United States after reading an article by Jacob Riis, a Danish-born journalist and photographer known for his muckraking work. Bissell aimed to raise funds for a sanatorium located on the Brandywine River in Delaware. By 1908, the program had expanded into a national initiative under the joint efforts of the National Association for the Study and Prevention of Tuberculosis (NASPT) and the American National Red Cross. Initially, the seals were sold at post offices in Delaware for one cent each, with the net proceeds being equally divided between the two organizations. By 1920, the Red Cross withdrew from the arrangement, and the sales of Christmas Seals were managed exclusively by the NASPT, which later became known as the National Tuberculosis Association (NTA). In the late 1960s, the organization changed its name to the National Tuberculosis and Respiratory Disease Association (NTRDA) to reflect its broader focus on respiratory health. In 1973, the NTRDA was renamed the American Lung Association, although the 1974 Christmas Seals still displayed the NTRDA inscription on the sheet margins. Today, the proceeds from Christmas Seals benefit the American Lung Association and support various lung health initiatives. While tuberculosis had been in decline for many years, it has recently shown a resurgence. Tuberculosis remains the most prevalent major infectious disease globally.
